# Māra Saṁyutta (SN 4)

**ID:** SN 4
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Māra Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0301m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mārasaṁyutta* (SN 4) is the fourth collection of the *Sagāthāvagga* in the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, comprising twenty-five discourses arranged into three chapters (*vagga*s), with ten suttas in each of the first two and five in the third [Bodhi 2003; Bingenheimer]. The collection consists of substantive narrative prose interspersed with verse, chronicling dramatic encounters between the Buddha and Māra, the god of temptation, deceit, and death. In these episodes, Māra manifests in frightening or deceptive guises—such as a serpent, an elephant, or an ox-herd—or taunts the Buddha with challenging verses, seeking to disrupt his concentration or incite doubt; in every instance, the Buddha recognizes him instantly and rebukes him in verse [Bingenheimer]. Prominent narrative settings include the banks of the Nerañjarā River shortly before and after the awakening, the failed seduction attempt by Māra's three daughters (SN 4.25), and the Maddakucchi Deer Reserve, where the Buddha mindfully endures agonizing pain after his foot is injured by a stone sliver sent by Devadatta (SN 4.13) [Bodhi 2003; Gaffney 2003; Samyutta Nikaya---The Grouped Discourses; Collett 2014]. The collection forms an early thematic pairing with the immediately following *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta* (SN 5), which continues identical confrontation narratives between Māra and enlightened nuns [Bodhi 2003; Kingsbury 2002].

 Substantial portions of the collection were preserved in Sanskrit Buddhist literature, being cited extensively in the *Mahāvastu-avadāna* [Lamotte 1988; Winternitz 1933; DharmaNexus] and aligned by DharmaNexus with texts including the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the *Lalitavistara*, and Tibetan versions of the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* and *Abhiniṣkramaṇasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pāli canon, DharmaNexus identifies thousands of matching segments, showing extensive textual reuse with the *Bhikkhunī Saṁyutta* (SN 5), the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), and several books of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* [DharmaNexus].
